marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q005.takeaway: Horseshoe kidney is a common congenital renal fusion anomaly; it is the source-keyed answer as the most common anomaly among the listed choices.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q005.displayText:
The horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidney.

During development, the kidney is initially located in the pelvic region. Later, the kidneys ascend due to the growth of the body in the lumbar and sacral regions. Sometimes, the kidneys are pushed so close to each other during their ascent that their lower poles fuse, forming a horseshoe kidney.

The source keys horseshoe kidney as the most common congenital renal anomaly among these options. Current references more specifically describe it as the most common congenital abnormality of the upper urinary tract.
emphasis: most common congenital anomaly of the kidney

rationales.a: Renal agenesis is absence of one or both kidneys; it is not the most common congenital renal anomaly in this source context.
rationales.b: Renal duplication is a collecting-system developmental anomaly, but the source identifies horseshoe kidney as the most common congenital anomaly of the kidney.
rationales.d: Pancake kidney is a rare fusion anomaly and is not the most common congenital renal anomaly.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q006.takeaway: The fused horseshoe kidney cannot ascend normally because its isthmus is caught beneath the inferior mesenteric artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q006.displayText:
The inferior mesenteric artery prevents the ascent of the horseshoe kidney.

The horseshoe kidney is usually found at the level of the lower lumbar vertebrae. Its ascent is halted by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery. The connecting isthmus of the horseshoe kidney may be present either in front or behind the aorta and the inferior vena cava.

Pelvic kidney: Occasionally, one kidney fails to ascend. It is usually found in the pelvis near the common iliac artery.

rationales.a: The inferior vena cava may relate to the horseshoe-kidney isthmus, but it is not the classic structure that arrests renal ascent.
rationales.b: The aorta is an important posterior relation, but the fused kidney is classically stopped by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery.
rationales.c: The ureter drains the kidney and does not mechanically prevent ascent of a horseshoe kidney.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q007.takeaway: Classically, the bladder trigone is formed by incorporation of the caudal mesonephric ducts into the posterior bladder wall.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q007.displayText:
The trigone on the posterior wall of the urinary bladder is formed by the incorporation of the lower ends of the mesonephric ducts.

After this incorporation, the ureters now open separately into the bladder, near the opening of the mesonephric duct. Due to the ascent of the kidneys, the ureteral openings move farther cranially, while the openings of the mesonephric ducts move close together. The triangular area between these ducts (trigone of the bladder) is thought to arise from the terminal portion of the mesonephric ducts.

Recent update: It was considered that the epithelium of the trigone is initially mesodermal and is later replaced by the endoderm-derived transitional epithelium. However, current research indicates that there is no mesodermal epithelial contribution to the bladder at the trigone (Gray's Anatomy, 41st edition).

rationales.b: Metanephric blastema forms nephron excretory components, not the bladder trigone.
rationales.c: The cloacal membrane temporarily closes the embryonic cloaca and does not form the trigone.
rationales.d: The urogenital sinus contributes most of the bladder, but the classic structural origin tested for the trigone is incorporation of the lower mesonephric ducts.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q008.takeaway: A midline cystic lesion between the umbilicus and bladder is a urachal cyst caused by persistence of a segment of the urachus.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q008.displayText:
A palpable fluid-filled mass that is connected to the umbilicus superiorly and urinary bladder inferiorly is diagnostic of the urachal cyst.

During embryonic development, the upper end of the urogenital sinus communicates with the allantois, which lies in the umbilical cord. The allantois normally regresses to form a fibrous cord called the urachus. In the adult, the urachus is seen as the median umbilical ligament.

The remnants of the urachus that may be seen after birth are shown in the source figure.

rationales.a: A vitelline-duct cyst is related to the omphalomesenteric duct and bowel, not a tract extending between the bladder and umbilicus.
rationales.b: A horseshoe kidney is a renal fusion anomaly and does not produce a fluid-filled midline urachal tract mass.
rationales.c: Polycystic kidney disease produces multiple renal cysts rather than a single midline cyst connected between the bladder and umbilicus.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q009.takeaway: Seminiferous tubules and rete testis arise from sex cords, whereas efferent ductules arise from mesonephric tubules.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q009.displayText:
The seminiferous tubules are derived from the sex cords.

The epithelium in the gonadal ridge proliferates to form the primitive sex cords. They multiply further under the influence of the SRY gene on the Y chromosome and penetrate deep into the medulla to form testis cords. Near the hilum of the testis, these cords break into a network of tiny cell strands, which later give rise to rete testis.

Various parts of the testis are derived as shown in the source table.

rationales.a: Mesonephric tubules contribute the efferent ductules, not the seminiferous tubules.
rationales.b: The paramesonephric duct largely regresses in males under anti-Müllerian hormone and does not form seminiferous tubules.
rationales.c: Primordial germ cells give rise to the germ-cell lineage within the testis but do not form the seminiferous-tubule framework.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q010.takeaway: The appendix of the epididymis is a Wolffian (mesonephric) duct remnant; the appendix of the testis and prostatic utricle are Müllerian remnants.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q010.displayText:
The appendix of the epididymis is derived from the Wolffian duct (mesonephric duct).

It is the most cranial portion of the Wolffian duct (mesonephric duct) and remains as a vestigial structure.

rationales.a: The prostatic utricle is a paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct remnant, not a Wolffian-duct derivative.
rationales.b: The appendix of the testis is derived from the cranial paramesonephric duct, not the mesonephric duct.
rationales.d: Rete testis develops from testis cords near the testicular hilum rather than from the Wolffian duct.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q011.takeaway: In males, the prostatic utricle and appendix of the testis are the key paramesonephric-duct remnants.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q011.displayText:
The prostatic utricle is derived from the paramesonephric duct (Mullerian duct).

In males, under the influence of the anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) produced by the Sertoli cells, the paramesonephric ducts degenerate.

Only two structures are derived from paramesonephric ducts in males:
• The appendix of the testis (also known as hydatid of Morgagni) is derived from the cranial end of the paramesonephric duct.
• The prostatic utricle (also known as utriculus prostaticus) is a small indentation in the prostatic urethra. It is located at the apex of the urethral crest, on the seminal colliculus (verumontanum), laterally flanked by openings of the ejaculatory ducts.

rationales.a: Paradidymis is a mesonephric-tubule remnant rather than a paramesonephric-duct derivative.
rationales.b: The trigone is classically related to incorporation of the lower mesonephric ducts, not persistence of the paramesonephric duct.
rationales.c: The appendix of the epididymis is a mesonephric (Wolffian) duct remnant, unlike the prostatic utricle.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q012.takeaway: Untreated bilateral cryptorchidism commonly causes sterility because the higher extrascrotal temperature impairs spermatogenesis.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q012.displayText:
Bilateral cryptorchidism usually results in sterility.

In this condition, both testes fail to descend into the scrotum. Therefore, the higher temperature to which they are exposed in the abdominal cavity will inhibit spermatogenesis. The majority of men with untreated bilateral cryptorchidism have azoospermia.

rationales.a: Impotence concerns erectile function; cryptorchidism primarily compromises spermatogenesis rather than necessarily causing erectile failure.
rationales.c: Male pseudo-intersexuality results from impaired masculinization despite a male genetic/gonadal sex and is not the usual consequence of bilateral cryptorchidism.
rationales.d: Female pseudo-intersexuality describes virilization of a genetic female and is unrelated to retained testes in bilateral cryptorchidism.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q013.takeaway: Male genital swellings form the scrotum; their female homologues form the labia majora.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q013.displayText:
The genital swellings in the male differentiate into the scrotum.

The genital swellings are a pair of elevations that develop on either side of the urethral folds. The genital swellings later become the scrotal swellings in the male, which give rise to the scrotum.

In females, they differentiate into the labia majora.

rationales.a: The testes develop from the gonadal ridges, not from the external genital swellings.
rationales.c: Most of the penile urethra forms through fusion of the urethral folds around the urethral plate, not from the genital swellings.
rationales.d: The glans penis develops from the genital tubercle rather than the genital swellings.

marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q014.takeaway: Hypospadias results from incomplete fusion of the urethral folds, producing an ectopic urethral opening on the ventral penis.
marrow__ANAT_CH10_Q014.displayText:
The given condition is hypospadias and it is due to the failure of the urethral folds to fuse completely.

The cloacal folds fuse:
• Cranially to form the genital tubercle
• Caudally they constitute:
  • Urethral folds anteriorly
  • Anal folds posteriorly

At the end of the third month, the two urethral folds close over the urethral plate forming the penile urethra.

In hypospadias there is an incomplete fusion of the urethral folds. The urethra opens abnormally on the inferior aspect of the penis usually near the glans, but it can open along the shaft or near the base of the penis. In rare instances, the urethral meatus opens in the scrotal area. If the urethral folds fail to fuse completely, a wide vertical slit can be present along the entire length of the penis and the scrotum. The two scrotal swellings then closely resemble the labia majora.

In epispadias, the urethral meatus is found on the dorsum of the penis. It is most commonly seen with exstrophy of the bladder and defects in the closure of the anterior body wall.

rationales.b: Failure of anterior abdominal-wall closure is associated with defects such as bladder exstrophy and epispadias, not the typical mechanism of hypospadias.
rationales.c: Genital swellings form the scrotum in males; their failure does not explain a ventral urethral opening.
rationales.d: The genital tubercle forms the phallus; hypospadias specifically reflects incomplete fusion of the urethral folds.
